strengths: Rigorous theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.3 is formally stated, completely proved, and provides novel sufficient conditions for port-Hamiltonian structure on meshes derived from first principles rather than assumed as a template

Principled principle-driven approach: Formalizing four physical requirements (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, energy balance) to deduce structural constraints is methodologically sound and eliminates non-physical degrees of freedom that competitors cannot

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple evaluation metrics, physics-consistency diagnostics, OOD generalization tests across frequency/resolution/parameter shifts, and rigorous ablations directly supporting theoretical predictions

Strong empirical results: Orders of magnitude better energy drift (1.3e-4 vs 5.9 for MGN), exact momentum conservation without explicit constraint, and improved OOD robustness with 169× fewer parameters than MGN
Automatic topological conservation: Hard-wiring incidence structure preserves constraints like ∇·B=0 mechanically without post-hoc regularization, eliminating spurious modes

Data efficiency and practical efficiency: Demonstrated improved data efficiency curves, favorable computational profile (fastest inference/training, smallest memory footprint), and O(N) sparse operations
Well-designed ablations: Table 9 directly validates the necessity of topology, orientation covariance, and metric positivity by selectively violating assumptions and observing degradation
weaknesses: State-independent coupling assumption is restrictive: Corollary 3.4 limits applicability to systems with state-independent incidence gains; Section 5.5 toy example is artificially constructed; no validation on realistic nonlinear systems with true state-dependent coupling (e.g., nonlinear acoustics, incompressible flow)

Limited real-world scope: Only one real dataset (The Well acoustic scattering); evaluation heavily dominated by linear wave equations, the 'easiest' continuum physics; no challenging nonlinear regimes (turbulence, multiphase, reactive flows)

Energy stability not rigorously proved in discrete setting: Theorem 3.3 establishes continuous-time energy inequality, but discrete stability depends on integrator (Strang splitting); formal proof of discrete energy stability is absent, only empirical demonstration

Incremental novelty over DEC literature: Topology-metric split is well-established in Discrete Exterior Calculus (Hirani 2003, Desbrun 2005); main contribution is systematic formalization and neural network connection, which while valuable is somewhat incremental

Limited insight into learned representations: Paper doesn't explore what Gθ and Rθ actually capture; can users interpret learned metrics? Does G_θ recover known material properties? Transfer to new materials/geometries is unexplored
Narrow experimental domain: Most experiments on periodic 2D grids or Delaunay triangulations; limited testing on unstructured/3D/adaptive meshes; acoustic scattering only non-synthetic domain

Incomplete analysis of design choices: Motivation for diagonal G_θ parameterization is pragmatic but may miss cross-channel couplings; CFL guard necessity and sensitivity not thoroughly analyzed; limited justification for MLP architecture choices

Theorem scope limitations: Requires Jacobian existence and local differentiability; doesn't apply to truly discontinuous systems (shocks, contacts); applicability to piecewise-smooth dynamics only on smooth regions

strengths: Principled theoretical framework: Theorem 3.3 elegantly derives topology-metric separation from physical principles (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, energy balance), with rigorous proofs (Lemmas B.1-B.4). The insight that structure is a consequence rather than an assumption is valuable.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive benchmarks spanning analytic plane waves, physics-consistency diagnostics, OOD generalization (frequency/resolution/parameter shifts), realistic data (The Well acoustic scattering), nonlinear systems, heterogeneous domains, and detailed ablations (D.6-D.9).

Strong empirical results: Consistent near-zero energy drift, correct wave dispersion, momentum conservation at 10^-7 scale without explicit constraints, superior data efficiency, and robust extrapolation across resolution and parameter shifts compared to MGN, HNN, and other baselines.

Exceptional ablation studies: Principle-level ablations (Sections 5.6-5.7, Appendices D.8-D.9) convincingly isolate effects of topology vs. metric factors. Scrambled-Topology and No-Orientation variants show catastrophic failure despite comparable one-step MSE, vindicating the theory.

Reproducibility: Detailed experimental protocols, hyperparameters in appendices, promised code release. Dense notation is supplemented by concrete examples (Appendix A, Maxwell's equations in C.1) and intuitive motivation (Figure 1).
Clear motivation: Articulates precisely why MeshGraphNets lack guarantees (missing orientation covariance and energy constraints), allowing spurious modes and non-physical degrees of freedom.
weaknesses: Limited scope of applicability: Theory assumes all four principles (L, P, O, E) hold exactly. Experiments focus on scalar wave equations and linear elastodynamics. Only one real-world experiment (acoustic scattering, still structured); no Navier-Stokes, MHD, or complex coupled PDEs. Unclear how to extend to systems with non-Hamiltonian components (viscosity, plasticity) or non-trivial thermodynamic structures (metriplectic, GENERIC).

Theorem 3.3 is local (Jacobian-level), not global: Reduction holds pointwise, not globally. Claims of 'near-zero energy drift' and momentum conservation are empirical, not theoretical guarantees. Long-horizon stability depends on time integration and, implicitly, discretization.

Restrictive architectural choices not fully justified: Quadratic metric G_θ adopted 'for efficiency' (§4) but not derived from theory. Section 5.7 shows state-dependent J improves accuracy, yet main model restricts to state-independent G_θ. Block-separable energy H(z)=H_k(z_k)+H_{k+1}(z_{k+1}) excludes coupled energies. Strang splitting chosen by convenience, not principle.

Limited real-world validation: The Well experiment is nearly Hamiltonian (small dissipation), on structured Cartesian grids with sponge-layer boundaries (not theoretically addressed). No unstructured 2D meshes, no 3D, no systems with complex industrial-scale heterogeneity or boundary conditions.

Insufficient comparison with related work: Baselines (MGN, HNN, FNO, GraphCON) are somewhat dated. HNN assumes canonical variables (different setup); MGN-HP uses soft penalty (not direct competitor). No direct comparison with recent GENERIC/metriplectic networks, bracket-based methods, or other modern data-driven exterior calculus approaches.

Theoretical gaps: Orientation covariance (O) is restrictive—not all systems admit global orientation (systems with interfaces, defects, broken symmetries). Energy balance (E) requires clean conservative/dissipative split, excluding complex thermodynamics. Permutation equivariance (P) may not hold in heterogeneous media with distinct regions. Extensions to these cases not discussed.

Missing practical guidance: No systematic guidance on applying MeshFT to new PDE systems (choice of cochains, state representation, boundary handling). OOD tests (Table 11) use only variations of 2D periodic waves; more diverse OOD scenarios (different mesh topologies, geometries) would strengthen generalization claims.

strengths: Mathematically sound reduction theorem (Theorem 3.3) with complete proofs establishing local port–Hamiltonian structure from physical principles; the derivation from L/P/O/E assumptions is principled and well-motivated

Exceptionally rigorous and comprehensive experimental validation including physics-consistency diagnostics (wave speed, canonical consistency, PDE residuals, equipartition, momentum conservation to ~10⁻⁸), multiple datasets (synthetic waves, acoustic scattering from The Well, nonlinear lattices), and extensive OOD generalization tests

Impressive empirical results: orders-of-magnitude better energy stability (drift 10⁻⁴ vs 5.9 for MGN), momentum conservation without explicit constraints, robust extrapolation across resolution and parameter shifts, 350× fewer parameters than baselines with faster inference

Well-designed ablation studies (Sections 5.6-5.7, Appendix D.9) convincingly demonstrate the practical necessity of topology-fixed structure and metric-dependent learning; separation of concerns is empirically validated
Clear presentation with excellent pedagogical choices (Figure 1 comparison, concrete Maxwell example in Appendix C, careful notation); the core insight about topology-metric separation is accessible
weaknesses: Theorem 3.3 is a local Jacobian-level statement at differentiable points, not a global guarantee on full dynamics; the remark explicitly states 'we neither assume nor claim the full dynamics admits a single global port–Hamiltonian representation,' significantly weakening claims. Gap between pointwise Jacobian factorization and observed long-horizon energy conservation remains theoretically unjustified

Incremental theoretical novelty over discrete exterior calculus: the topology-metric split is established in DEC literature (Hirani 2003, Desbrun et al. 2005) and data-driven variants (Trask et al. 2022). The contribution is applying this principle through physical axioms and learning, but geometric justification already exists

Critical restrictive assumptions under-explored: state-independent incidence gains (Corollary 3.4) assumed universally despite Theorem 3.3 allowing state-dependence; block-separable convex energies exclude coupled systems; practical necessity of orientation covariance underdeveloped (Table 14 shows violations harm but scale varies)

Severely limited experimental scope: all tests remain within comfort zone—plane waves, synthetic lattices, one 2D acoustic scenario. No demonstration on turbulence, multiphase flows, truly nonlinear materials, anisotropic/anelastic systems, or realistic 3D problems where topology-metric split's real value would emerge

Significant gaps in experimental comparisons: baselines are dated (MGN/HNN/FNO from 2019-2021); missing recent structured learning methods, graph neural operators with conservation, equivariant PDE networks. Method uses hard-wired mesh topology while baselines learn from scratch—comparison is unfair but not acknowledged. MGN-HP with penalty is a weak baseline; better would be methods with hard-coded conservation

Data efficiency claims conflate structure with data: 'data size' counts only trajectory pairs, not mesh topology information which is structural knowledge. Method trades learned data for domain knowledge; presenting this as pure data efficiency is misleading. Low-data regime comparison (<100 pairs) unclear

Reproducibility concerns: code not provided for review; 29-page paper with key details scattered across 17-page appendix; some hyperparameters relegated to 'released code'; dense technical content makes verification difficult

strengths: Novel principle-driven reduction theorem (Theorem 3.3) elegantly derives port-Hamiltonian structure from four physical axioms, avoiding rigid global templates
Exceptional physical fidelity: near-zero energy drift (10^-4 to 10^-5), momentum conservation at 10^-7 scale, and correct dispersion emerge structurally without explicit constraints

Comprehensive experimental validation spanning analytic benchmarks, physics-consistency diagnostics (5 metrics), OOD generalization (frequency/resolution/parameter shifts), real acoustic data, and extensive ablations
Superior data efficiency and robustness: maintains physics fidelity with fewer training samples and remains stable under OOD shifts where baselines diverge (Table 5)
Exceptional reproducibility with code to be released, detailed hyperparameters, multiple random seeds, and clear data generation procedures throughout appendices
Practical efficiency: O(N) sparse operations, substantially fewer parameters than baselines (642 vs 100k+), faster inference/training, lower memory (Table 15)
Clear presentation with excellent motivation, well-structured proofs, informative figures (especially Figure 1), and honest treatment of limitations
weaknesses: Limited scope of applicability: framework excels on linear/weakly nonlinear wave-like systems; unclear generalization to turbulence, phase transitions, strongly nonlinear materials, or systems with memory effects

Jacobian-level rather than global guarantees: Theorem 3.3 proves local (pointwise) reduction, not that full trajectories follow port-Hamiltonian form; Strang splitting integrator and CFL-guarding are not uniquely determined by theory

Limited real-world validation: The Well acoustic scattering is primary real dataset (single system); most validation on synthetic data with known structure; lacks validation across diverse physical domains

Restricted practical assumptions: quadratic, state-independent energy metric limits nonlinear constitutive laws; general nonconvex energies discussed but not explored; state-dependent coupling remains limited (Section 5.7)

Insufficient guidance on applicability: lacks systematic characterization of when method succeeds vs. fails; no validation that real physical systems actually satisfy the four axioms (e.g., empirical orientation covariance)
Scalability questions: all experiments 2D or small-scale; no 3D demonstrations; impact on large-scale problems unclear

Incomplete experimental scope: nonlinear benchmarks limited to polynomial lattice systems without Navier-Stokes or complex materials; no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis; mesh quality effects unexplored
